children: The latest GREED & fear report points to rising private capex, electrification, advanced manufacturing and energy demand as key structural themes for India

India’s structural growth story could remain resilient even as investor focus on artificial intelligence and related infrastructure evolves, according to Jefferies’ latest GREED & fear report, titled The Virtues Of Small Over Large.

The report argues that while the global AI investment cycle is generating significant spending on data centres and computing infrastructure, India’s growth drivers extend well beyond the technology theme. Private sector capital expenditure, electrification, renewable energy, advanced manufacturing and rising electricity demand are emerging as important areas of focus.
AI Investment Faces Questions Over Capacity
The report raises questions about the scale of capital expenditure planned by major US hyperscalers as AI infrastructure investment accelerates.

Jefferies notes that consensus estimates currently point to around USD 990 billion of capex by four major hyperscalers in 2027. The report questions whether such a level of spending will ultimately be required, particularly as companies explore more efficient ways of deploying AI computing capacity.

The report also cites research indicating that Anthropic server utilisation had declined 26 per cent from its January 2026 peak, while cautioning that the finding comes from third-party research and should be interpreted accordingly.

Another theme highlighted is the development of small language models (SLMs). Citing a Stanford University study, Jefferies notes that SLMs are narrowing the performance gap with large language models while requiring substantially lower energy and computing costs.
The report suggests this could encourage greater use of on-premises AI systems by companies, potentially reducing dependence on centralised cloud infrastructure for certain applications.
India’s Structural Growth Drivers

Against this backdrop, Jefferies points to several areas supporting India’s longer-term growth. A separate Jefferies report on India’s “new industrial revolution” identified six areas combining policy support and rising private sector participation: space, semiconductors, solar manufacturing, data centres, electronics and aerospace.
The report notes that government support for these sectors is visible through measures including incentive schemes, tax holidays and localisation requirements.

The growth of global capability centres is another indicator cited in the report. India added 111 greenfield GCCs in the first eight months of 2026, according to data referenced by Jefferies, with these centres expected to create around 70,000-75,000 jobs.
Office demand has also strengthened, with net absorption rising from 21 million sq ft in 2021 to 61 million sq ft in 2025 and an estimated 60 million sq ft in 2026.
Electrification Emerges As A Key Theme
Energy and electrification are highlighted as another major structural opportunity for India.
Jefferies points to the expansion of renewable energy, particularly solar power, and the development of battery storage as important components of the country’s future electricity infrastructure.

The report draws comparisons with China, where the expansion of the electricity grid and improvements in battery storage have helped bring down the cost of solar power. It suggests that similar developments in India could support the country’s manufacturing ambitions by reducing the cost of electricity over time.
The report also cites projections from Hitachi Energy India that total final energy demand could increase by 50 per cent and electricity demand by 100 per cent by 2035, reaching 3,365 TWh.

As a result, electricity’s share of total final energy demand is projected to rise from 19 per cent in 2023 to 25 per cent in 2035, supported by growth in renewables, energy storage and smart demand management.
Private Capex Shows Signs Of Recovery
The report also highlights signs of a long-awaited recovery in private sector capital expenditure in India.
India’s annualised nominal gross fixed capital formation-to-GDP ratio increased from a recent low of 31.4 per cent in the four quarters to December to 32.4 per cent in the four quarters to June.
At the same time, machinery imports have increased substantially, rising from USD 29 billion in FY21 to USD 62 billion in FY26 and USD 66 billion in the 12 months to August 2026.

Jefferies also notes that India is already a major global producer across several traditional manufacturing categories, including crude steel, cement, ammonia, mobile phones and solar modules, although production remains significantly below China’s levels in several of these industries.
The report therefore places India’s manufacturing opportunity within a broader combination of domestic demand, policy support, private investment and infrastructure development.
India’s Growth Story Beyond The AI Cycle
The report’s broader message is that India’s structural growth drivers are not dependent solely on the global AI investment cycle.

While AI remains a major technology and investment theme, Jefferies highlights electrification, renewable energy, manufacturing, private capex and infrastructure as areas that could continue to shape India’s economic trajectory.

The report also makes clear that its views represent Jefferies’ research assessment and that the investment themes discussed carry risks and uncertainties. It does not constitute personalised investment advice.
